source.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka SAEs

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAEs recover and disentangle features in Gemma-2-2B activations, extending the claim's indirect-evidence version to a real language model; it does not reproduce the original toy-network method.
record.gate_note: The post also reports reconstruction performance, downstream cross-entropy, and automated interpretability scores. These do not directly measure the claim versions and are omitted. The reported SAE feature-recovery, splitting, composition, and concept-probing outcomes are included.
record.test_reason: The post compares an SAE architecture of its own with BatchTopK SAEs. Its absorption, splitting and meta-SAE composition results bear on V5. Standard BatchTopK latents absorb hierarchical features more as the dictionary grows, split concepts, and share decoder information. The decomposition also changes with SAE architecture. This argues that SAE latents are not canonical, atomic units. The TPP, SCR and k-sparse probing rows are benchmark scores for the authors' method against a baseline, not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. One addition: the authors say Matryoshka SAEs better match intuitive general-to-specific feature ordering. They call the method a promising step toward better monosemantic representations, with mixed k-sparse probing and autointerp results needing further work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses nested sparse autoencoders on Gemma-2-2B activations, comparing Matryoshka SAEs with BatchTopK SAEs; it does not use the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE architecture and dictionary size affect absorption, splitting, composition, and probing outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Matryoshka SAEs outperform BatchTopK on TPP and improve on SCR with dictionary size. k-sparse probing results are mixed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchically regularised SAEs yield latents better suited for targeted concept erasure than standard SAEs.

record.problems: Only one Matryoshka SAE was trained. Several relevant outcomes are qualitative or approximate, with no uncertainty estimates or detailed per-size values in the post. Results concern SAE representations of one model layer, not the underlying model's full feature geometry.
record.rows_left_out: Reconstruction, downstream cross-entropy, and automated interpretability results were omitted because they do not directly measure the claim versions. The post gives no exact per-dictionary-size values for the included qualitative comparisons.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, geometry, or sparsity transition.
All of it: no analysis of capacity or feature importance.
Whether the model's features are sparse and spread across neurons. The post uses SAEs as a tool and reports no neuron-level or model-side evidence.
Completeness, and stability across seeds or models. Only one Matryoshka SAE was trained, on one layer of one model.

missing.what: Matryoshka has worse MSE and variance explained, yet similar downstream cross-entropy at the largest sizes. This shows that the reconstruction-optimal dictionary is not the one closest to what the model uses, which is relevant to V5's canonicality.
Autointerp scores of 0.84–0.88 across all SAEs, with early Matryoshka groups slightly higher and later groups slightly lower.

record.verdict_notes: This is an architecture post on the Alignment Forum (Bussmann, Leask, Nanda), not peer reviewed. Results are mostly read off figures; only the absorption rates (~0.03, ~0.29) and autointerp range are stated numerically. It could arguably be classed T4, since it is mainly method performance. I treated it as T5 for V5 only, because the absorption and composition results on standard SAEs directly argue that SAE latents are not canonical or atomic units.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or from competition between important and less important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The post evaluates SAE features on one model and selected tasks; it does not establish how features are distributed across neurons generally or across LLMs.
It measures shared information/composition in decoder directions, but does not test feature completeness, stability across conditions, or canonicality across methods or models.
Whether the represented features are one-dimensional rather than multi-dimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured first-letter feature absorption using the SAEBench task.

conditions.value: increases; exact sizes not attached to individual results

rows.measure: Fraction of probe true positives absorbed into single latents
rows.value: around 0.03; described as consistently very low across dictionary sizes
rows.note: The post says first-letter features remain mostly unabsorbed under this SAE architecture.
rows.check: This is absorption in SAE latents, not evidence that the model contains recoverable sparse features (V4). It bears on V5: low absorption (~0.03) holds only under the Matryoshka architecture, so latent quality depends on the training objective.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured first-letter feature absorption using the SAEBench task.

conditions.value: larger models; exact sizes not attached to individual results

rows.measure: Fraction of probe true positives absorbed into single latents
rows.value: increases with dictionary size, reaching approximately 0.29 for larger models
rows.note: The post reports increasing absorption for BatchTopK, though not that all first-letter information is absorbed.
rows.check: Relinked from V4 to V5. BatchTopK absorption rises with dictionary size to ~0.29. Latents warp hierarchical features, so they are not stable canonical units across dictionary sizes.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Used k-sparse probing on first-letter tasks to assess feature splitting.
rows.measure: Distribution of first-letter features across latents
rows.value: First-letter features remain almost entirely unified.
rows.note: No numerical splitting rates are provided.
rows.check: Relinked from V4 to V5. Unified first-letter features appear only under the Matryoshka architecture. The result is qualitative, with no rates given.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Used k-sparse probing on first-letter tasks to assess feature splitting.
rows.measure: Distribution of first-letter features across latents
rows.value: First-letter features frequently split across multiple latents.
rows.note: No numerical splitting rates are provided.
rows.check: Relinked from V4 to V5. BatchTopK latents frequently split single concepts, against canonical units. The result is qualitative only.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Trained meta-SAEs on the SAE decoder matrices and compared reconstruction of decoder directions.
rows.measure: Variance in decoder directions explained by meta-SAE
rows.baseline: BatchTopK SAE decoder directions; exact value not stated
rows.value: Substantially less variance explained than for BatchTopK SAE decoder directions.
rows.note: The post interprets this as less shared information and greater disentanglement, but gives no numerical values.
rows.check: Matryoshka decoder directions are more disentangled, but no values are given and the result is relative to BatchTopK only.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Trained meta-SAEs on the SAE decoder matrices and compared reconstruction of decoder directions.
rows.measure: Variance in decoder directions explained by meta-SAE
rows.baseline: Matryoshka SAE decoder directions; exact value not stated
rows.value: Meta-SAEs explain substantially more variance than for Matryoshka SAE decoder directions.
rows.note: The post interprets this as more shared information and composition among BatchTopK decoder directions.
rows.check: Meta-SAEs explain substantially more variance in BatchTopK decoders, so those latents are composed rather than atomic. The state should be absent for atomicity, not partial.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated concept isolation with Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP).

conditions.value: multiple counts; exact values not stated

rows.value: Consistently outperforms BatchTopK across nearly all dictionary sizes and numbers of ablated latents.
rows.note: The post describes this as better concept isolation; it does not provide scores here.
rows.check: TPP benchmark of the authors' method against a baseline. It measures SAE usability, not any version's effect.

conditions.value: multiple counts; exact values not stated

rows.note: The post does not provide scores here.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B

rows.check: SCR benchmark of the authors' method. This is method performance, not a test of a version.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated SAE features as concept probes using k-sparse probing.

rows.value: Mixed results; performance does not increase monotonically with dictionary size.

relationships.condition: BatchTopK SAEs on Gemma-2-2B layer 8 across dictionary sizes 2304–36864
relationships.reason: Absorption rises to ~0.29 with dictionary size (r2). Concepts frequently split (r4). Meta-SAEs reconstruct decoders well, so latents are composed rather than atomic (r6).
relationships.display_finding: Feature absorption rose with dictionary size to about 0.29, concepts often split across latents, and meta-SAEs reconstructed the decoders well, so the latents are composed rather than atomic.

relationships.condition: Matryoshka vs BatchTopK SAEs on the same activations
relationships.reason: Absorption (~0.03), splitting and composition all change with the SAE objective (r1, r3, r5), so the recovered units depend on an architecture choice.
relationships.display_finding: Absorption (about 0.03), splitting and composition all differed with the SAE objective, so the recovered units depended on an architecture choice.
